10.0.0.en: "The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother" [1]

10.0.1.en: At the beginning of chapter ten we read "The proverbs of Solomon," or, as it appears in some old copies of the Vulgate, "The Second Book of Proverbs."

10.0.2.en: Some regard the preceding chapters (Prov 1-9) as a kind of introduction to the book, revealing the importance of wisdom and its blessings.

10.0.3.en: In these chapters we listen to Wisdom as she calls us to enter her house, to be united with her, and to live by her, so that we are enlightened in every action and under all circumstances. She also calls us not to listen to folly, for it is deceitful and turns us aside from the way of truth. The preceding chapters did not deal with the problems we face in their details; rather, they set out the broad lines and the spirit in which we should walk. They concentrated in a special way on the young, that they might attach themselves to wisdom and reject folly.

10.0.4.en: Now with chapter ten he begins to present the proverbs. Each proverb is short, but it has its weight in a person's life. For this reason this section needs a quiet reading, mingled with prayer and with striving to practice the wise life.

10.0.5.en: Some think that the body of the book begins with chapter ten, where this section deals through proverbs with the situations to which the believer is exposed. Others think that Holy Scripture as a whole, in all its parts (the Law, history, wisdom, and prophecy), is in harmony with this section and closely bound to it, and that these books offer practical examples throughout history that reveal the work of the Wisdom of God in us and its riches, as well as examples of those who reject wisdom and cling by their own will to folly.

10.0.6.en: Who is the father who is gladdened by his wise son? And who is the mother who grieves over the foolish son?

10.0.7.en: a. According to the literal interpretation, the wise man here means the father and the mother by blood, for they see in their son their hope in life that he will inherit from them, not only in their wealth and their experience of life, but also in their fellowship with God in Christ Jesus by the Holy Spirit. Without doubt the conduct of the son or the daughter is reflected in the parents' state of mind, but the wisdom of the son fills the father's heart with even more gladness, for he is proud of him, and perhaps turns to him as to a younger brother who shares counsel with him, and he may entrust to him the management of all his property with a glad heart. But the folly of the son or daughter is reflected even more on the mother, because she is more emotional than the father and cannot bear the ruin or loss of her children.

10.0.8.en: If the wise Solomon speaks to us of the wise son who brings joy to his father, he himself is an example of this (1 Chr 22:12; 2 Chr 1:7-12), and as for the mother who grieves over her son's folly, an example is Rebekah, who tasted bitterness from the folly of her son Esau (Gen 26:34-35; 27:46).

10.0.9.en: b. Since Solomon appears in this book as a father speaking with every member of his people as his son, the father and mother here are every person who feels an obligation toward those under his charge. Whether he is a king, a ruler, or a teacher, he does not seek to dominate, command, and forbid, but offers fatherhood or motherhood in love, so that all those around him may enjoy the wise life of faith.

10.0.10.en: c. If every believer in a position of leadership feels a fatherhood or motherhood toward those around him, how much more the bishop and the priest, who enjoy fellowship in the unique priesthood of the Lord Christ. With the Apostle Paul he bears bowels burning with love for the salvation of every soul and for bringing it into the fellowship of the heavenly glories.

10.0.11.en: * Be obedient to your bishop, and welcome him as a father to your soul... And I also say that bishops must know that they are priests and not lords... It is a bad custom that spreads in some churches that priests are bound to keep silent in the presence of bishops.

10.0.12.en: St. Jerome d. Evangelical Church teaching is a fatherly work, in which the priest gives not the juice of his thought but his whole life, in order to bring every person out of the corruption of the world into the glory of the children of God. This is what the Apostle Paul meant by his words: "I have begotten you through the gospel in Christ Jesus" (1 Cor 4:15).

10.0.13.en: * When a person learns from the mouth of another, he is called the son of the one who teaches him, and the latter is counted his father.

10.0.14.en: St. Irenaeus * The word is the child of the soul; therefore we call those who teach us our fathers... and the one who learns in submission is counted a son.

10.0.15.en: St. Clement of Alexandria e. Every true believer, under all circumstances and regardless of his age, carries in his depths a kind of fatherhood or motherhood, so his soul longs to see all humanity enjoying the blessed evangelical life that he enjoys.

10.0.16.en: f. But what is above all this is that we have the heavenly Father, who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4). If a father desires to make his son happy, offering all his resources, even his health and his time, for his happiness, then the father on his part is happy at his son's success. The happiness is shared between the wise father and the son who walks in wisdom. So God, the source of wisdom, offered His Wisdom (the Son) incarnate and given up for us, to raise up from us wise sons, and to find His pleasure in us as we become His icon and walk after His likeness in the spirit of wisdom. And just as the heavenly Father is pleased with His Son if he walks in the spirit of wise sonship, so the Church, as a mother, grieves over every soul marked by folly, because in her tender motherhood she wishes to raise every human soul to the glories prepared for it. The Church bears us in her womb as her members, who are fit to bear her wisdom, being like the Bridegroom, the Wisdom of God Himself, and sharing in His nature.

10.0.17.en: In other words, the wise man, though his soul rejoices and exults in God's work in him, God the giver of wisdom, the Lord of heaven Himself rejoices, as do the hearts of his family and all who love him; but if he turns aside to evil in folly, he loses his inner joy and grieves the hearts of many. Thus the wise Solomon uses every means to urge us to enjoy wisdom and to forsake folly.

10.1.s.en: 2. The wise man's wealth of righteousness

10.1.0.en: 2 Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death.

10.1.1.en: Perhaps someone will say: "I seek what is for myself; my father's pleasure does not concern me, and my mother's grief does not pain me. I am not a child; I care for what pleases me." Therefore the wise man affirms that all that a person gathers in his wickedness and folly profits him nothing.

10.1.2.en: "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from evil" [2]

10.1.3.en: The portion of the righteous is happiness, life, and satisfaction, but the portion of the unbeliever is bitterness, death, and hunger. This righteousness is considered the introduction to all the virtues mentioned in this section.

10.1.4.en: Wealth that a person acquires by illegitimate means will not last; it quickly vanishes. And at the moment of death it does not support its owner.

10.1.5.en: The wicked man may be rich, but his treasures do not satisfy his depths, nor do they give him inner peace, so he always feels want. The righteous man, though poor, is made by God to need no one and nothing, and God gives him spiritual and psychological satisfaction with protection from evil. Righteousness delivers its owner from death, since for him it becomes a passage to a meeting with God face to face. The believer sees in the righteousness of Christ a victory over death and a triumph over Hades.

10.1.6.en: The prophet Jeremiah speaks to us of the wicked rich man who relies on his riches and gathers what he can by improper means, saying: "The partridge broodeth over what it hath not laid; he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool" (Jer 17:11). So the foolish rich man embraces money and possessions, things that God gave to man to share with his brothers, and thinks them his alone; he toils and loses, and at the end of his life, when he leaves behind all that he gathered, he discovers that he was a fool. But the righteous man, whatever troubles and pains he suffers in this life, escapes eternal death.

10.1.7.en: The story of Esther presents a practical picture fulfilled throughout history: Haman, who had authority and wealth, lost everything, and evil surrounded him, while the godly Mordecai was glorified by God in this world and enjoys eternal glories.

10.1.8.en: * "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing" (see Prov 10:2). What then? Have not some escaped death by paying money (like one who pays a ransom so that he is not killed or sentenced to death)? Certainly this happens. But they cannot be cleared of sin, and in truth they prepare for themselves a life worse than death. Therefore we must not put our trust in wealth but in virtue... As for righteousness, it not only delivers those who possess it, but also leads many others to desire it, and continually transfers them from death to eternal immortality.

10.1.9.en: St. John Chrysostom * If a man casts his seed on ground full of thorns and abundant weeds, covered with the refuse of the harvest, he suffers a double loss. He loses his first seed, and he also suffers much toil. Therefore, in order that the divine seed may flourish well in us, let us first remove from our hearts worldly cares and the useless anxiety that makes us seek to be rich, for "we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Tim 6:7). For what profit is there in possessing superfluous things? "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing: but righteousness delivereth from death" (Prov 10:2).

10.2.0.en: "The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish: but he thrusteth away the desire of the wicked" [3]

10.2.1.en: The Lord does not allow the soul of the righteous to die of hunger, because it is He who feeds it, offering His word, the bread of life. The psalmist says: "I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread" (Ps 37:25).

10.2.2.en: It is not material, psychological, or social resources, or the circumstances surrounding each of them, that satisfy the heart of the righteous or leave the heart of the wicked hungry; rather the heart of the believer is lifted up as to the heavenly table, so that his depths exult in the midst of the tribulations that come upon him, while the depths of the wicked turn into an emptiness with nothing to satisfy it.

10.2.3.en: The men of God have sung of this satisfaction, and have also warned the wicked of the state of famine, hunger, and thirst that comes upon them. We recall, for example:

10.2.4.en: As for me, I will behold thy face in righteousness: I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with thy likeness (Ps 17:15).

10.2.5.en: The meek shall eat and be satisfied: they shall praise the LORD that seek him: your heart shall live for ever (Ps 22:26).

10.2.6.en: They shall not be ashamed in the evil time: and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied (Ps 37:19).

10.2.7.en: My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips (Ps 63:5).

10.2.8.en: Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple (Ps 65:4).

10.2.9.en: Man did eat angels' food: he sent them meat to the full (Ps 78:25).

10.2.10.en: O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days (Ps 90:14).

10.2.11.en: With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation (Ps 91:16).

10.2.12.en: Who satisfieth thy life with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's (Ps 103:5).

10.2.13.en: He watereth the hills from his chambers: the earth is satisfied with the fruit of thy works (Ps 104:13).

10.2.14.en: The trees of the LORD are satisfied; the cedars of Lebanon, which he hath planted (Ps 104:16).

10.2.15.en: That thou givest them they gather: thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good (Ps 104:28).

10.2.16.en: Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing (Ps 145:16).

10.2.17.en: He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the fat of the wheat (Ps 147:14).

10.2.18.en: A covetous man's eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the wickedness of the wicked drieth up his soul (Sir 14:9).

10.2.19.en: * "And filleth thee with the fat of the wheat" (Ps 147:14). Note that he did not say "wheat" only, but "the richest fat of the wheat," pointing to great abundance, the most abundant of fruits. For the gifts of God are like this, as you see, exalted and flourishing. He speaks of them here as giving satisfaction from the best kinds of wheat and in overflowing generosity, to show that He does not merely give to you, but satisfies you.

10.2.20.en: * He gives not merely food, but what is profitable for everyone, what everyone desires, and what satisfies everyone.

10.2.21.en: St. John Chrysostom * Do you fear that your inheritance will run short if you begin to give generously from it? Where has it ever happened that the resources of a righteous person failed, when it is written: "The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish" (Prov 10:3)?

10.2.22.en: Elijah was fed by the ravens in the wilderness.

10.2.23.en: And a meal was prepared from heaven for Daniel in the pit, when he was shut in by the king's command to be prey for the lions, and you fear that you will lack bread... The Lord Himself rebuked in the Gospel those who have doubt in their thought and whose faith is weak, saying: "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?" (Mt 6:26).

10.2.24.en: God feeds the birds, offering daily food to the sparrows and to creatures that have no sense of divine things and do not need food or drink. Can a Christian then lack anything?! Can the servant of the Lord lack? Can one who practices good works, and who is dear to the Lord, lack?!

10.2.25.en: St. Cyprian If God is the supreme eternal Good, then the wealth of this world cannot satisfy the soul that is in the image of its Creator; rather, its union with God, and its enjoyment of His dwelling in it, satisfies it and fills it with joy.

10.2.26.en: * O my poor soul, what are you seeking?!

10.2.27.en: If you want wisdom, you will find Jesus, the source and fountain of wisdom, indeed Wisdom Himself!

10.2.28.en: If you seek strength and power, He is the Almighty!

10.2.29.en: If you search for pleasure and delight, He is the fountain of true joy!

10.2.30.en: If you long for intoxication, His love intoxicates the soul!

10.2.31.en: If you hunger for bread, He is the bread of life!

10.2.32.en: If you are passionate for riches, He is the Creator of all!

10.2.33.en: If you want rest, you will find your rest in Him alone...! Receive Him, for you have no one else to satisfy you.

10.3.0.en: 4 He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich. 5 He that gathereth in summer is a wise son: but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame.

10.3.1.en: "He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich" [4]

10.3.2.en: The wise man is always at work and in motion, gathering riches. The fool is lazy, preferring sleep and slackness to watchfulness and diligence, and his portion is poverty.

10.3.3.en: God created Adam and set him in Paradise to work, for He blesses the diligent hand, and in His providence allows the slack hand to become poor, for whoever does not work shall not eat. Whoever sows neglect reaps poverty, and whoever sows zeal and diligence reaps blessing and success.

10.3.4.en: Work and the ability to do it are a gift that God gives to man, so it is fitting for the believer not to stop working as long as he can, and as far as the strength, ability, and talents God gives him allow. The call to work has come as a command of Scripture. The Apostle says: "For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you; neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you" (2 Thess 3:7-8). It is as though a serious and practical desire to work accompanies living faith and expresses it.

10.3.5.en: The land that the farmer does not toil to plow and sow yields thorns instead of grapes or other fruits and crops. The earth, with all its rich resources, does not give us fruits or treasures without work, such as farming, prospecting for mines of precious metals, and fishing... for the earth could not have been fit for life if work had not been practiced.

10.3.6.en: Most of the governments of the world have recognized the danger of unemployment and idleness for the behavior of society, and so they have counted unemployment the most dangerous enemy that threatens society and robs it of its peace. For work is not only a source of increased production, but also of the growth of man's character and his inner peace.

10.3.7.en: The joyful message of the Gospel came as a clear call to work without ceasing, by the riches of God's grace, that man may reach the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, that is, that the believer remain striving all the days of his sojourn to taste the sweetness of the inner Kingdom.

10.3.8.en: * In the beginning God gave us a life free from cares and exempt from toil. But we did not use the gift well; we spoiled our rest and lost Paradise. For this reason He made our life wearisome... Idleness works to corrupt us and causes us many troubles.

10.3.9.en: * In the beginning you could have worked without toil... because God Himself wanted this, but you did not allow it. For God did not mix work with toil. If man had experienced toil from the beginning, he would not have been afflicted with it afterward as a punishment. In fact you can work and at the same time not reach the stage of hard labor, as in the case of the angels.

10.3.10.en: St. John Chrysostom * Let us contemplate the fear of God in the lives of these saints. Yes, we find that it is written of Moses and Aaron that they worked and lived with men who walked after their example, and so too Joshua the son of Nun.

10.3.11.en: A letter attributed to St. Clement of Rome * The good worker receives the wages of his work with boldness, but the lazy and the negligent does not dare to look his employer in the eye.

10.3.12.en: St. Clement of Rome * Everyone who comes to you in the name of the Lord, receive him (Mt 21:9; Ps 118:26); after that test him and get to know him, so that you may distinguish the right hand from the left.

10.3.13.en: If the one who comes is a traveler passing through, help him as far as you are able, but he should not stay with you more than two or three days if necessary.

10.3.14.en: If he wants to stay with you as a craftsman, let him work in order to eat (2 Thess 3:10).

10.3.15.en: But if he has no trade, then direct him yourselves, so that he does not live among you as an idle Christian.

10.3.16.en: If he does not want to work, he is a trafficker in Christ (1 Tim 6:5); beware of such people.

10.3.17.en: The Didache The text in the Septuagint reads: "Poverty brings a man low, but the hands of the diligent make rich"

10.3.18.en: * It is said: "Poverty makes a man humble" [4 LXX]. And Christ also says: "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Mt 5:3). Do you grieve because you are on the road that leads to virtue? Do you not know that this gives us great confidence (He cares for us in spite of our poverty)?!

10.3.19.en: St. John Chrysostom * It is said: "Poverty brings a man low"; by poverty he means stinginess, by which the rich man becomes poor, having nothing to offer to others.

10.4.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria "He that gathereth in summer is a wise son: but he that sleepeth in harvest is a son that causeth shame" [5]

10.4.1.en: Here the wise Solomon blames the one who does not seize the right opportunity for work, for if a man is negligent in the season of harvest, he loses his labor that he did during the sowing. It is as though it is fitting for a man to labor not only in the season of plowing and sowing, taking care of the crop, but also in the summer, the time of harvest. The Lord Christ urged His disciples to work, saying to them: "Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest" (Jn 4:35).

10.4.2.en: The wise man portrays our life on earth as sons working in our Father's vineyard. It does not befit us to sleep at the time of harvest, and so be counted sons of disgrace and shame; rather we should work and gather, and as the Apostle says: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). It is a precious time for work in our Father's vineyard. The Apostle Paul gives us a practical example of working without ceasing, while Demas represents the man who sleeps at harvest time. "For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica" (2 Tim 4:10)

10.5.0.en: "Blessings are upon the head of the just: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked" [6]

10.5.1.en: The righteous man walks uprightly, submits to counsel, and obeys commands in the Lord, so his portion is blessedness and safety. The unbeliever walks in crooked ways, deceitful and in inner terror, and his end is destruction.

10.5.2.en: Although the world cannot bear the righteous, it is only for a time, and these will surely receive many blessings in their depths in this world, and openly in the world to come. But as for the wicked, their mouth, filled with violence, testifies against them and deprives them even of temporal blessings; their mouth condemns them!

10.5.3.en: The law of the harvest is that what a man sows he reaps, so whoever sows uprightness reaps the blessings of God and the praise of others. But whoever sows the tares of sin, injustice and violence rule his mouth, and his words come forth from a corrupt heart.

10.6.s.en: 6. The memory of the wise man

10.6.0.en: "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot" [7]

10.6.1.en: The righteous and the wicked both die, but their destiny differs, and even their remembrance differs, for the memory of the righteous remains a blessing to many, while the name of the wicked becomes like a garment eaten by moths. For after nearly twenty centuries we find no Christian who calls his son Judas, but we find many who call him "Paul."

10.6.2.en: Paul stood alone before a dangerous lion roaring to devour him, the unjust Nero. But he saw the Lord standing before him, whose eternity and remembrance death cannot destroy: "Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom" (2 Tim 4:17-18).

10.6.3.en: After the death of the prophet Elisha, when the raiders of Moab cast a man into his grave, and the body touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood up on his feet (2 Kgs 13:21). So his memory bore a power that appeared from his bones! And the Lord Christ said of the woman who broke the alabaster flask of ointment and poured it on His head: "Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her" (Mk 14:9). And St. Mary said: "For, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" (Lk 1:48).

10.6.4.en: The memory of the righteous remains carrying the sweet fragrance of Christ, and offers blessings through the generations, so we should not be surprised to see St. Gregory of Nazianzus lament his brother St. Caesarius, not denying human feelings, but asking that they be with moderation. He says: [Even in my tears and admiration I must respect the law that governs these things, for this is not foreign to our philosophy. It says: "The memory of the just is accompanied by blessings." And let tears also flow from our eyes, and begin with lamentation, as those who have suffered a great loss (by his death), and so remove from us insensibility and excess.]

10.6.5.en: * "The memory of the just is praised." He did not say this to mean that our praise helps the departed souls. Rather he said it because those who praise the departed receive the greatest benefit from their remembrance. Therefore, since we gain much benefit from their holy remembrance, let us not despise the words of the wise man, but rather give heed to them.

10.7.0.en: "The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall" [8]

10.7.1.en: When the heart of the believer is filled with heavenly wisdom, as the Wisdom of God dwells in him, he bows down before Him with his whole being, and his soul exults in obedience to the divine commandment. But the fool thinks himself wise, and does not want to listen to the divine voice, but in stubbornness insists on his own thought.

10.7.2.en: Since Abraham, the father of fathers, was wise, "when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went" (Heb 11:8). So Abraham and his sons according to the Spirit found joy and gladness in obedience to the commandment.

10.7.3.en: The man who is wise in his heart turns his knowledge into action, so he receives the commandments and fulfills them, for he longs to hear and obey in the Lord. He thirsts for the word of the Lord like the thirsty land that longs for water to quench it and turn it into a paradise. But the fool in his words brings forth empty words that do not support him but cause him to fall.

10.8.0.en: "He that walketh uprightly (in simplicity) walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known" [9]

10.8.1.en: The upright man is always secure; he is marked by simplicity, has no two faces or two personalities, and walks uprightly without fear, because there is no place in his life for hypocrisy or craftiness. But whoever perverts his ways, thinking he can hide his deceits, will surely have them discovered and his affair exposed.

10.8.2.en: Joseph walked uprightly in his father's house, and was a faithful and upright servant in the house of Potiphar the Egyptian, and was faithful even as a prisoner, and so lived in security despite the tribulations that came upon him and pursued him. And at last he sat as the second man in Pharaoh's palace. All this commends him before God, to live forever in the divine embrace in heavenly peace and eternal security.

10.8.3.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that uprightness here means simplicity, in which the believer lives with a simple mind, not composite or complicated, walking the straight way and not limping between this way and that.

10.8.4.en: * We do not recommend that we acquire a simplicity without knowledge, so that we yield to everything that is said and are deceived by every deceitful teaching, but we mean by simplicity that whose whole meditation is on virtue, God, and goodness, like the child who knows only one teacher and fears him alone, and carries out only his command, and does not accept the teaching of any other teachers.

10.8.5.en: So the believer ought to be a child in his conduct with Christ, with His fear ruling his life, and not accept teaching from any other teacher. For childhood is pure by nature, and no tyranny corrupts the mind of the child.

10.8.6.en: Let us now rejoice in discipleship to Christ in the way He has shown us, and strive to walk in simplicity and be children in order to receive good teaching. And let us be wise as serpents against the enemy who schemes to harm us, and remember at all times the saying of our Lord that whoever does not receive the Kingdom of God as a child will not enter it (Lk 18:7). May the Lord make us worthy of it, to whom be glory for His greatness. Amen.

10.8.7.en: St. Mar Philoxenos * "Blessed is every simple (upright) soul" (see 11:25 LXX), "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9].

10.8.8.en: For this is the cause of all kinds of evil, that many do not know how to apply the commandment uprightly, even the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. So in this case the writer does not mean by (simplicity) the foolish man, or the one who knows nothing, but the one who is free from evil, who is not a doer of evil, for he is wise.

10.8.9.en: * Was not the Gospel first preached to the shepherds (the simple)? And also to Joseph, who, being simple in mind, did not allow the suspicion of adultery to frighten him into committing a wrong? Did not God choose the simple, men who are sincere by nature? For it is written: "Blessed is every simple soul," and also "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9].

10.8.10.en: You say: "True, but prudence is required."

10.8.11.en: I ask you: "What is simplicity if not prudence?!" For when you do not suspect men, and do not pretend anything, when you have no disturbances and cannot remember the harm!

10.8.12.en: * Absalom was a deceitful man who stole the hearts of all men (2 Sam 6:15). Note how great his deceit was, for it is recorded that he would come forward and say: "Hath no man judged thee?" wishing to win everyone over to himself. But David was innocent. What then? Look at the end of both. See how the first was full of madness! For since he concentrated wholly on harming his father, he was struck blind in everything, because "he that walketh uprightly walketh surely" (Prov 9:10).

10.8.13.en: St. John Chrysostom Let the insincere listen to what is written: "He that walketh in simplicity walketh surely" [9]. Truly simplicity of conduct is a guarantee of security. Let them warm themselves with what the mouth of the wise man says: "Deceit flees from the discipline of the Holy Spirit" (Wis 1:5). Let them also hear what the testimony of Scripture affirms: "his strong relationship (his secret) is with the upright" (Prov 3:32), for God's strong dealings are His disclosure of His secrets to human minds by the enlightenment of His presence.

10.8.14.en: "But he that perverteth his ways shall be known"; in contrast to simplicity, deceit, or walking in a crooked way. The deceitful think that by their experience and skills they are able to deceive others and not be discovered. But "there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad" (Mk 4:22). Judas planned with the Pharisees to betray the Lord Christ, and thought that his affair would not be discovered, but what he did in secret carried a scandal on the level of earth and heaven, and across the centuries.

10.9.0.en: "He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall" [10]

10.9.1.en: We have already spoken of the last part of this verse (see [8]). The text in the Septuagint reads: "He that reproves with boldness makes peace." The text in the Syriac agrees with the Septuagint. Whoever rebukes sin faithfully and openly supports the peace of the community more than one who ignores it or does not care about it. For many sinners return to God through a word of rebuke full of frankness and love, especially if the rebuke is joined with a spirit of tenderness and humility. Although rebuke wounds the feelings of the sinner, its being mingled with love and tenderness drives him to sincere repentance.

10.9.2.en: Winking with the eye points to deceit and cunning, and anciently it pointed to corrupt glances that stir up fleshly desires.

10.9.3.en: Some think that winking of the eyes indicates that what he utters is other than what he conceals within, or that what he says is other than what he thinks. Others think that the kiss of Judas to the Lord Christ at His betrayal was a kind of deceit like winking of the eye.

10.9.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria sees it as a form of adultery, in which a person expresses the desires of his body with his eyes. For the glances and movements of the eye reveal either the inner enlightenment or the hidden desires of the flesh.

10.9.5.en: * The amorous, mocking glances, which are winks of the eyes, are nothing but the commission of adultery by the eyes, for lust is fought through the eyes. For of the whole body the eyes perish first. "The eye that contemplates the beauty of things gladdens the heart," meaning that the eye that sees uprightly rejoices.

10.9.6.en: "Winking the eye with deceit gathers woes for men." These practice the effeminacy of Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, who sat on his throne with his feet raised up, daintily fingering his purple robe, and rolling the whites of his eyes upward. So do women who practice the same thing, displaying their desire for sin through their glances.

10.9.7.en: And as Scripture says: "The light of the body is the eye," so the radiance of the light appears through inner enlightenment.

10.9.8.en: "The adultery of a woman is in the lifting of the eyes" (Sir 26:9).

10.10.0.en: "The mouth of a righteous man is a well of life: but violence covereth the mouth of the wicked" [11]

10.11.0.en: The mouth of the wicked is full of violence and deceit, stirring up quarrels, and his portion is punishment and destruction. But the speech of the righteous is a source of rest and knowledge for his hearers, offered in the spirit of love [12]. His portion is the fellowship of goodness with others and the storing up of knowledge and wisdom.

10.11.1.en: The mouth of the righteous is always spoken through by the Lord who dwells in him, as it was said to the prophet Moses: "Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say" (Ex 4:12). And to the prophet Jeremiah: "I have put my words in thy mouth" (Jer 1:9). Therefore he overflows with living waters, that is, words useful for teaching, comfort, and guidance.

10.11.2.en: The expression "a well of life" in Hebrew means "overflows in the arteries of life," as though the mouth of the righteous man becomes like the heart that receives the impure blood and beats to pour out pure blood into the arteries of the whole body. So no evil or harmful word comes out of the mouth of the righteous, but he overflows with words of divine life, so that everyone who meets him finds rest and enjoys God's work in him.

10.11.3.en: The Lord Christ, who dwells in the spiritual man, is manifested in all his words, and presents him as a mystery of life to others.

10.11.4.en: The spiritual man lives in the likeness of his Lord, so that his whole heart beats with life without ceasing for the life of others and their growth in every aspect of their lives.

10.11.5.en: The mouth of the righteous is like a well that overflows with sweet water on the surrounding land and waters it, as it quenches the thirst of people, animals, and birds.

10.11.6.en: As for the last part of the verse, it was discussed earlier (verse 6).

10.11.7.en: If the mouth of the righteous is like a spring, overflowing with the waters of the Spirit on those around him, turning deserts into gardens full of fruit, the mouth of the wicked is like a sea full of turbulence, casting from its depths salt water on the shores. The sound of its currents never calms, night or day, and not even grass can grow on its shores, and if it overflows with its waters on a cultivated field, it ruins all its crop!

10.11.8.en: So from every person's mouth comes what overflows from his heart, either sweetness that gives life and growth, or saltiness that destroys life and sends forth death.

10.11.9.en: This phrase reminds us of the Lord Christ's words to the Samaritan woman: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38).

10.12.0.en: "Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins" [12]

10.12.1.en: If the wise Solomon has linked wisdom with righteousness, the third of them is love, without which a person loses the spirit of wisdom and divine righteousness. He also links folly with evil, and the third is hatred, for folly and evil have their source in the closing of the heart and its rejection of love, and at the same time they feed hatred and make it grow. Hatred is their cause and their source, and it grows and flourishes by them.

10.12.2.en: In the spirit of hatred a person remembers past events that stir his soul and urge him to quarrels, and he cannot forget even after tens of years, and cannot forgive the faults of his brothers. But the spirit of love is like beautiful curtains that cover the faults and mistakes of others, and therefore he does not boil inside because of them. If love "beareth all things," keeping the peace of the soul and the unity of the community, hatred stirs up the soul, which stirs up disturbances within, and disputes and quarrels without. Hatred seeks to find an opportunity to stir up enmity, for it finds its pleasure in divisions and quarrels, but love gives harmony and reconciliations, and removes from every soul the evil provocations, so that the person finds his delight in building up his brothers, pouring water on every flame to extinguish it.

10.12.3.en: Both the Apostle James and the Apostle Peter quoted this phrase. "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). "For charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8).

10.12.4.en: * He who has love considers no one a stranger, but considers all as his kin and family, and knows no anger, and is not arrogant, and does not burn with fury, and does not wrong, and does not rob another of his honor, and never counts anyone his enemy except the devil alone.

10.12.5.en: Mar Ephrem the Syrian * Just as our enemy divides the brothers who are still weak and carnal by a sudden outburst of anger over some trivial causes and earthly matters, so he sows the seed of strife even among spiritual persons on the basis of differences in thought, and from these there certainly arise disputes and struggles with words, which the Apostle condemns... By these our malicious and dangerous enemy sows strife between brothers who were of one mind. For the words of the wise Solomon are true: strife begets hatred, but friendship is a fortress for all who do not fight.

10.13.0.en: 13 In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding. 14 Wise men lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction.

10.13.1.en: "In the lips of him that hath understanding wisdom is found: but a rod is for the back of him that is void of understanding" [13]

10.13.2.en: The speech of the man of understanding supports others, but the fool benefits no one, and succeeds only in drawing punishments to fall upon himself.

10.13.3.en: He who bears wisdom in his heart as in his mind, wisdom announces its presence through his words, so his mouth is blessed and his lips are a storehouse of wisdom. But the one who is void of understanding, that is, one able to learn who does not want to learn, the rod is his teacher, falling on his back so that he bends down broken. In other words, whoever does not seek wisdom and knowledge from a burning, loving heart prepares his back for harsh blows, and bends down by force and in bitterness.

10.13.4.en: Perhaps the lives of both Solomon himself and his son Rehoboam illustrate this proverb. The first did not rely on his personal wisdom, but asked wisdom from God, and many came from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom and benefit. "And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, which had heard of his wisdom" (1 Kgs 4:34). But Rehoboam relied on his human wisdom and the counsel of his young friends, and did not consult God, nor accept the counsel of the elders, and because of him the kingdom was divided, and the rod of discipline fell on his back (1 Kgs 12:8-19).

10.14.0.en: "Wise men lay up knowledge: but the mouth of the foolish is near destruction" [14]

10.14.1.en: The wise man is skillful: whenever he finds knowledge, he stores it in his depths, especially the word of God, hiding it and guarding it by a godly, holy life, so that when he needs it he finds it not far from him but within him. He lays up knowledge through living, practical faith with prayer and earnest study of the word of God, so that he may enjoy the Lord Christ, the Wisdom of God, and possess Him, saying with the holy soul: "I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me. I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Song 3:4-5).

10.14.2.en: The wise man keeps knowledge in order to speak it at the right time, in the right place, in a fitting manner, and to the right person.

10.14.3.en: Since the wise man understands the value of words, he counts them as jewels that must be stored in a safe place, but the fool does not cease from speech that has no meaning, which brings him near to destruction. You do not know what he will say, because he brings out words without balance, bringing upon himself and others countless troubles.

10.14.4.en: For the sake of a man's peace and the building up of his brothers, it is fitting for him to think much and speak little, and not utter a word without thought preceding it.

10.14.5.en: St. Timothy represents the wise man who is rich in true knowledge: "But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim 3:14-15). On the contrary, Elymas the sorcerer represents the arrogant fool who destroys himself (Acts 13:6-11).

10.14.6.en: * St. Paul says: "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above." And he adds: "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory" (Col 3:1-4).

10.14.7.en: Life according to the flesh disappears in us if our base nature blames us, and then we transfer the ambition of our life from earth to heaven. As the proverb says: "Wise men lay up knowledge" (Prov 10:14). Then we wait for the true life, and Christ appears in us and we are filled with His glory, and are changed into a holy state.

10.14.8.en: Let us now listen to the words of the Song, as though we had died in the body, so that we are not drawn to words with a fleshly meaning. The person who has died to the passions turns the literal meaning of the words of the Song into pure and undefiled meanings. And since his mind is empty of earthly things, his mind is occupied with the things above, where Christ is, free from passion, sitting on the right hand of the glory of God (Col 3:1). Let us now listen to the words that describe the pure beauty of the bride. May we listen as though we did not share in the nature of the body, but had passed over into the realm of the Spirit.

10.15.0.en: "The rich man's wealth is his strong city:

10.15.1.en: the destruction of the poor is their poverty" [15]

10.15.2.en: This proverb is not advice that the wise man offers, but a statement of a regrettable reality, in which the rich man sees in his wealth his fortified city, and so is all the more fond of enlarging his possessions, while the poor man, seeing the rich man robbing him of his rights, collapses and has no motive to be delivered from the state of poverty that holds him captive.

10.15.3.en: Some think that this proverb means that the rich grows richer and the poor grows poorer. That is, the truly rich man strives all the more without ceasing, and the careless poor man persists in his carelessness without commitment or a sense of responsibility.
